Question: Which estimator performs best in the presence of noisy confounders and how does it compare to the Covariate Control (CC) estimator?
Evidence:
[E1] (text, Section 5.1, page 12): the fact that it suﬀers from higher variance. IPW has a large bias comparable to the naive estimator. The DR estimator’s performance falls in between OR and IPW. In scenario 2, we relax our assumption on the ability to observe the true confounders. Instead, we assume that we can only observe transformations of the true confounders as given in Eq. (15)-(16). This corresponds to a case where the researcher cannot directly observe X , but can still access a set of variables that are related to the confounders themselves (and thus will likely misspecify the model). Results and boxplots are given in Table 3 and Figure 6, respectively. Our ﬁrst observation is the dramatic drop in the performance of OR. The estimator performs the worst in both bias and MSE. DR achieves the best performance in this case with respect to bias, however it once again suﬀers from large variance. The AB estimator seems to provide a balance between bias and variance.
[E2] (text, Section 5.1, page 13): estimator 7 (AB) [20], and an entropy balancing 8 based method (EB) [9]. The main diﬀerence between ATE and ATETR estimation is the latter utilizes data among respondents only. Results and boxplots are given in Table 4 and Figure 7, respectively. In our tests, the OR estimator has the largest bias. The estimator is trained using controlassigned survey respondents, and counterfactuals for the treatment assigned respondents are generated using the trained model. In our setting, the OR estimator consistently underestimates counterfactuals for the treatment-assigned respondents, resulting in a bias that is comparable with the naive estimator. CC, EB and IPW have small biases; EB and CC estimators have the best MSE performance across all estimators. In scenario 2, we relax our assumption on our ability to observe the true confounders, and we assume that we can only observe transformations of the true confounders as given in Eq. (15)-(16). Results and boxplots are given in Table 5 and Figure 8, respectively.
[E3] (text, Section 5.1, page 10): We implemented four diﬀerent estimators and compared their performance under two diﬀerent scenarios. In scenario 1, we assume that we can observe the actual values of the confounding factors, i.e. , X 1 , X 2 . This allows us to correctly specify a model to adjust for all of the confounding variables, and Assumption 1 holds. Our ﬁrst estimator is a naive mean comparison among respondents. By deﬁnition this is an inconsistent estimator and does not take into account observed confounders. The remaining estimators are based on Lemma 1, and use the observed covariates to correct for the underlying bias. We implemented outcome regression (OR) [3], inverse propensity weighing (IPW) [13], a doubly robust (DR) estimator based on OR and IPW [3], and an adversarial balancing based estimator (AB) using Logistic Regression as the classiﬁer [20]. We measured the performance of each estimator via bias, median absolute error (MAE), and mean squared error (MSE) 6 as discussed in [13]. Results are given in Table 2. See Figure 5 for the distribution of estimates.
[E4] (table, Table 5, page 15): Table 5: Performance of diﬀerent ATETR estimators when noisy confounders are observed. Estimators are Adversarial Balancing (AB), Covariate Control (CC), Entrophy Balancing (EB), Inverse Propensity Weighing (IPW), Naive mean comparison and Outcome Regression (OR). Similar to the results in Ta- ble 4, EB outperforms across all measures. Similar to Table 4, simple CC estimator provides a comparable performance to EB.

[E5] (figure, Figure 8, page 15) (image attached): Figure 8: Performance of diﬀerent ATETR estimators when noisy confounders are observed. Estimators are Adversarial Balancing (AB), Covariate Control (CC), Entrophy Balancing (EB), Inverse Propensity Weighing (IPW), Naive mean comparison and Outcome Regression (OR). Similar to the results in Ta- ble 4, EB and CC outperform across all measures. IPW suﬀers from large variance, OR performs worse than naive estimator.

claims.text: The Entropy Balancing (EB) estimator performs best in the presence of noisy confounders, as it has the lowest bias and MSE among the estimators.
The Covariate Control (CC) estimator provides a comparable performance to the Entropy Balancing (EB) estimator in terms of bias and MSE.
The Outcome Regression (OR) estimator performs worse than the naive estimator in terms of bias and MSE.
The Inverse Propensity Weighing (IPW) estimator suffers from large variance, as indicated by its wide boxplot in Figure 8.
